params.question: Corneal endothelial cells can regenerate to replace those lost during intraocular surgery.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is false. Corneal endothelial cells are post-mitotic — they cannot divide or regenerate. Once lost, they are gone permanently. When the count falls below approximately 500 cells/mm², the Na-K-ATPase pump fails, water floods the stroma, and bullous keratopathy results. This is why preoperative endothelial cell counts by specular microscopy are essential before any intraocular surgery.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — this statement is false. Corneal endothelial cells are post-mitotic and do not divide. The starting count of roughly 2,500 cells/mm² only declines over a lifetime. Every intraocular surgery risks further irreversible loss, which is why a preoperative specular microscopy count below 1,000 cells/mm² warrants caution and below 500 cells/mm² risks bullous keratopathy.

params.question: A farmer from rural India presents with a corneal ulcer 10 days after injury by a vegetable thorn. Slit-lamp examination shows a dry, grey-white infiltrate with feathery margins and satellite lesions. Which feature most reliably distinguishes this from bacterial keratitis?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Rapid onset is characteristic of bacterial keratitis, not fungal. A bacterial infiltrate typically reaches maximum size within 24–48 hours — this patient's subacute 10-day course points away from a bacterial cause.

Correct. Feathery margins with satellite lesions are pathognomonic of fungal keratitis. Bacterial keratitis produces a dense, creamy-white infiltrate with ill-defined margins — never feathery edges or satellites.
Reduced corneal sensation is the hallmark of herpes simplex keratitis, where the virus damages corneal nerve endings, producing characteristic hypoaesthesia.
A ring infiltrate with radial keratoneuritis — inflamed corneal nerve branches — is the classic pattern of Acanthamoeba keratitis, typically seen in contact-lens wearers exposed to tap water.

overallFeedback.feedback: The distinguishing feature is feathery hyphate margins with satellite lesions — pathognomonic for fungal keratitis. In rural India, fungal keratitis is the dominant type after vegetative trauma. The critical treatment error is prescribing antibiotics instead of natamycin 5%.

Correct! Feathery hyphate margins and satellite lesions are pathognomonic for fungal keratitis. In rural India, fungal keratitis dominates after vegetative trauma. Natamycin 5% hourly is first-line — prescribing antibiotics alone here causes preventable corneal blindness.

interactions.label: A patient has a Schirmer's test result of 15 mm wetting and a tear film break-up

params.question: A patient has a Schirmer's test result of 15 mm wetting and a tear film break-up time of 5 seconds. What type of dry eye does this combination suggest?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Aqueous-deficient dry eye is indicated by Schirmer's wetting below 10 mm, reflecting insufficient lacrimal secretion. This patient's Schirmer's result of 15 mm indicates normal aqueous output.

Correct. Normal Schirmer's wetting (above 10 mm) with a reduced break-up time (below 10 seconds) indicates adequate aqueous production but an unstable tear film — the hallmark of evaporative dry eye, most commonly from meibomian gland dysfunction.

Combined dry eye shows both reduced Schirmer's wetting (below 10 mm) and reduced break-up time (below 10 seconds). This patient's normal Schirmer's result rules out a significant aqueous-deficient component.

Reflex hyperlacrimation is a symptom of dry eye, not a separate diagnosis. When the tear film is unstable, the lacrimal reflex floods the eye with aqueous tears that evaporate quickly — producing the paradox of watery yet gritty eyes.

overallFeedback.feedback: Schirmer's ≥10 mm rules out aqueous deficiency; TBUT <10 s confirms tear film instability. Together they indicate evaporative dry eye, most commonly from meibomian gland dysfunction.

Correct! Normal Schirmer's (≥10 mm) with reduced TBUT (<10 s) points to evaporative dry eye. Meibomian gland dysfunction is the commonest cause. Treatment follows a stepladder: lubricants, then cyclosporine drops, punctal plugs, and biologics.

interactions.label: On slit-lamp examination, a corneal scar is visible only under the slit-lamp bea

params.question: On slit-lamp examination, a corneal scar is visible only under the slit-lamp beam, and the iris pattern behind it is clearly seen. What grade of corneal opacity is this?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. A nebula is the faintest grade of corneal opacity — visible only on slit-lamp examination, with the iris clearly seen through it. It results from superficial scarring with minimal collagen disorganisation.
A macula is moderately dense — visible in direct light (not only under the slit-lamp beam), with the iris still discernible but not as clearly as through a nebula.
A leukoma is a dense, solid white opacity that completely hides the iris. It represents full-thickness scarring with severe collagen disorganisation.

An adherent leukoma is a leukoma with iris tissue physically stuck to the back of the scar, typically following a perforating corneal injury. The iris is not merely hidden but adherent to the posterior surface.

overallFeedback.feedback: This is a nebula — the faintest grade, seen only under the slit-lamp beam with the iris clearly visible. Remember the progression: nebula → macula → leukoma → adherent leukoma, reflecting increasing collagen disorganisation replacing the regular lattice.

Correct! The three main grades in order of increasing density are nebula (faint, slit-lamp only), macula (moderate, visible in direct light), and leukoma (dense, iris hidden). An adherent leukoma adds iris adhesion after corneal perforation.

params.question: Before removing a metallic foreign body from the cornea at the slit-lamp, you perform a Seidel test. Under cobalt blue light, a green rivulet of fluid streams from the wound site. What is the correct next step?

answers.text: Proceed with removal using a 23-gauge needle at a tangential angle

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A positive Seidel test means the cornea is perforated — aqueous humour is leaking through the wound. Attempting removal would enlarge the perforation and risk catastrophic intraocular damage.

answers.text: Instil proparacaine and use a sterile burr to remove the rust ring

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A sterile burr is used 24–48 hours after successful removal of a superficial foreign body, to clear a softened rust ring. With a confirmed perforation, no bedside manipulation should be attempted.

answers.text: Shield the eye and refer urgently for surgical repair

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. A positive Seidel test — a green rivulet of aqueous streaming through the wound under cobalt blue light — confirms full-thickness corneal perforation. The eye must be shielded with a rigid protector (never a pressure patch) and the patient referred urgently for surgical repair.

answers.text: Apply a pressure eye pad with antibiotic ointment and review in 48 hours

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A pressure pad over a perforated eye could force intraocular contents out through the wound. A positive Seidel test is a surgical emergency requiring urgent referral, not observation.

overallFeedback.feedback: A green rivulet of fluorescein-stained aqueous under cobalt blue light confirms full-thickness perforation. The correct action is to shield the eye with a rigid protector (not a pressure pad) and refer urgently for surgical repair. Never attempt bedside removal of a perforating foreign body.

Correct! A positive Seidel test (green rivulet = aqueous leak) confirms perforation. Shield the eye with a rigid protector — never a pressure patch — and refer urgently. Only superficial foreign bodies with a negative Seidel test are safe to remove at the slit-lamp.
